ambrosial

am-BROH-zhul -- from Greek/Latin ambrosia ('food of the gods') + -ial: something ambrosial tastes fit for a god. · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

To be ambrosial is to be extremely pleasing to the taste or smell.

The chef's grandmother made an ambrosial stew that filled the whole house with the smell of roasted garlic and rosemary.

Example

Every holiday, the bakery on Fifth Street fills the block with an ambrosial scent of cinnamon and butter that draws customers in from three streets over.

Ambrosial describes a smell or taste so wonderful it seems almost too good for ordinary food -- notice the sensory, food-and-scent-specific focus, not just "good."

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

delectable: Delectable means wonderfully delicious -- elegant, refined praise for genuinely excellent food. Ambrosial is even more extravagant: it suggests god-like deliciousness, a taste or smell almost too good for ordinary tables. A pastry chef makes many delectable desserts but perhaps one truly ambrosial creation.

heavenly: Heavenly praises anything that feels blissful -- a heavenly nap, a heavenly view, a heavenly pie. Ambrosial is narrower and more literary: it belongs almost solely to taste and smell, to food or scent so sublime it seems meant for the gods.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

foul: disgustingly unpleasant to taste or smell

nauseating: causing a feeling of sickness

Where it sits · how intense the deliciousness is

tasty → ambrosial → heady

tasty vs. ambrosial: Tasty is a mild, everyday word for food that's simply good; it sits at the bottom of the scale, far below ambrosial's almost unearthly deliciousness.

heady vs. ambrosial: A heady aroma goes even further than ambrosial -- ambrosial promises delight almost too fine for ordinary food, while heady means the scent is so rich and overwhelming it leaves you dizzy.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — ambrosi-: the food and drink of the gods (Greek/Latin ambrosia)

suffix — -al: having the qualities of; pertaining to

Put it together: Ambrosial comes from ambrosia, the mythical food and drink of the Greek gods, said to grant them eternal youth, plus this unit's suffix -al ('having the qualities of'). Something ambrosial tastes or smells so wonderful it seems fit for the gods themselves.

Use the root in a new word: ambrosia: The word ambrosia turns up in nearly every collection of Greek myths on the library shelf.

Root Check

Word Choice

Ambrosial is a poetic, almost old-fashioned word -- reserve it for food or scent that is not just tasty but sublime; using it for something ordinary like plain toast would sound like exaggeration played for laughs.
